prompt: According to the lesson, what is a metric?

choices.text: A number that anybody computing correctly will reproduce
choices.why: Three teams computed correctly and got three numbers; the number depends on the definition.

choices.text: A definition
choices.why: Right. The number is what the definition produces on a given day.

choices.text: The column a dashboard sums
choices.why: The column is one of five parts; the filter, the time and the owner are the others.

choices.text: Whatever the finance team reports, since it is audited
choices.why: Finance's figure answers finance's question; marketing's answers another, and is not wrong.

prompt: Match each figure for the first quarter of 2026 to the team that reports it.

pairs.right: finance: money that arrived and stayed

prompt: Why does marketing include refunded orders in its revenue?

choices.text: Its query has a bug
choices.why: The lesson calls none of the three wrong; each answers its own question.

choices.text: Because finance has not yet confirmed the refunds
choices.why: The refunds are in the data; marketing includes them on purpose.

choices.text: It measures demand, and a refunded order was still demand
choices.why: Right. Its question is how much its campaigns produced, not how much money stayed.

choices.text: Because refunded orders are excluded later, when the quarter closes and the books are audited
choices.why: Nothing in its definition removes them later.

prompt: How many reais separate marketing's figure, R$ 329,036.20, from finance's, R$ 294,209.60?
Order 5002 has a gross value of 29,610 cents and 15% off. What `discount_cents` does the view compute?
Finance decides the shop should round discounts the other way. What does the view make possible?

choices.text: One line changes and every number built on it moves
choices.why: Right. The arithmetic is written once, so it changes once.

choices.text: Old reports are recomputed and archived automatically
choices.why: A view computes when queried; it archives nothing.

choices.text: No change; PostgreSQL fixes the rounding
choices.why: The view's expression decides it, and it can be written either way.

choices.text: Each dashboard can choose its own rounding without affecting the others
choices.why: That is the opposite of the point: one rule, read by all.

prompt: `CREATE VIEW order_revenue` fails with `relation "order_totals" does not exist`. Why?

choices.text: `order_revenue` must be created before `order_totals`
choices.why: It is the other way round: it reads from `order_totals`.

choices.text: The shop was reset since lesson 1, which dropped the earlier view
choices.why: Right. Re-running `lantern.sql` drops the schema with its views; create `order_totals` again first.

choices.text: Views cannot read from other views
choices.why: They can, and this one does.

choices.text: You are connected to `postgres`
choices.why: Possible but not the likeliest; the lesson names the reset.

prompt: Match each part of finance's net revenue to its value.
In which parts do marketing's and finance's revenue definitions differ?
hint: Compare what is summed and which rows take part.

choices.text: Aggregation and time
choices.why: Both sum, and both use the order date in São Paulo.

choices.text: The owner, and nothing else
choices.why: The owners differ, and so does the arithmetic.

choices.text: In the five parts, since the teams wrote separate queries
choices.why: Aggregation and time are the same.

choices.text: Measure and filter
choices.why: Right. Gross against net, and no filter against paid without the test account.

prompt: Two numbers with the same name disagree. What does the lesson say to compare first?

choices.text: The two queries, line by line
choices.why: The queries are long and hide the difference; the parts are short.

choices.text: The parts of each definition
choices.why: Right. The difference fits in a couple of cells of the anatomy table.

choices.text: The dashboards' refresh times
choices.why: That explains a lag, not a definition.

choices.text: Who has more seniority
choices.why: Seniority decides nothing about arithmetic.

prompt: Why does the lesson count the owner as a part of a metric when it is not arithmetic?

choices.text: Because the owner computes it every month
choices.why: Anybody may compute it; the owner decides what it means.

choices.text: Because dashboards display the owner's name next to every number shown on the screen
choices.why: Not the reason given.

choices.text: Without one, the definition drifts with every edited query
choices.why: Right. With an owner, a change is a decision with a date.

choices.text: Because the law requires a named owner for revenue
choices.why: No such rule is involved.

prompt: In "net revenue by region and month", region and month are each a ___.
Two reports map states to regions with their own `CASE`, and one puts Bahia in a different region. What happens?

choices.text: PostgreSQL refuses the second mapping
choices.why: Nothing stops two queries from disagreeing.

choices.text: They disagree about two regions and both look right
choices.why: Right. The mapping is a definition, and lesson 3 moves it into a table every query reads.

choices.text: Totals for the whole country change
choices.why: The national total is the same; only the split between regions moves.

choices.text: Only the North is affected, since Acre is small
choices.why: Bahia's region and the one it moved to are both affected.

prompt: How many paying customers does the North region have in Lantern's data?
A customer ordered in February from Paraná and moved to São Paulo in March. A report groups February's orders by the customer's current state. What is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing, since the customer is the same person
choices.why: The person is the same; the attribute at the time of the order is not.

choices.text: The order is counted twice, once per state
choices.why: One row, one state; it is moved, not doubled.

choices.text: Past figures shift retroactively
choices.why: Right. Whether a dimension shows its value at the time of the event or now is part of its definition.

choices.text: Paraná's revenue grows retroactively
choices.why: Paraná loses the order; it does not gain one.

prompt: What is the difference between `channel` in `customers` and `channel` in `web_sessions`?

choices.text: How the customer first arrived, against where one visit came from
choices.why: Right. One is recorded once at signup; the other changes with every visit.

choices.text: None; they hold the same four values
choices.why: Same values, different things described.

choices.text: One is in cents and the other in reais
choices.why: Neither is money.

choices.text: `web_sessions` is the newer, corrected version
choices.why: Neither corrects the other; they describe different events.

prompt: A dashboard divides orders by customer channel by visits by session channel to get "conversion per channel". What is wrong?

choices.text: Visits must be counted per day first
choices.why: The problem is not the time grain.

choices.text: Orders and visits use different time zones
choices.why: Both are in the same database setting.

choices.text: Conversion should be expressed in points
choices.why: Units are not the issue.

choices.text: The two halves are grouped by different things
choices.why: Right. Nothing joins first-arrival channels to visit sources, so the ratio means nothing.

prompt: A dimension that means the same thing in every table carrying it is called ___.
On 31 May 2026 Lantern has 705, 1,308 or 2,482 active customers. What decides which is right?

choices.text: The largest, since it misses nobody
choices.why: "Ever ordered" only grows; it is not an activity measure.

choices.text: The shop's buying rhythm
choices.why: Right. The window should match the shop's rhythm, which the gaps between orders measure.

choices.text: Which one finance reported last quarter, for continuity
choices.why: Continuity matters once a definition exists; it does not choose the window.

choices.text: The smallest, to be conservative
choices.why: Thirty days calls many regular customers gone.

prompt: What is the median number of days between a Lantern customer's consecutive orders?
Two people quote different "active in the last 30 days" numbers from the same dashboard. What is the likeliest reason?

choices.text: The dashboard caches results per user
choices.why: Possible in some tools, but not the lesson's point.

choices.text: One of them excluded the test account
choices.why: One customer cannot explain much.

choices.text: They looked on different days, and the window moves daily
choices.why: Right. A monthly report fixes the as-of date.

choices.text: 30 days is ambiguous between calendar and business days in every database
choices.why: The query uses calendar days; the moving date is the difference.

prompt: Excluding customer 1 makes no visible difference to 1,308 active customers. Why exclude it anyway?

choices.text: The definition says so
choices.why: Right. A definition applied only when it matters is not a definition.

choices.text: Because a query that leaves it in runs a lot slower on large tables
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Because the test account would otherwise be counted twice in every period
choices.why: `count(DISTINCT customer_id)` counts it once at most.

choices.text: Because it has no orders in May
choices.why: Then excluding it changes nothing and still applies the rule.

prompt: Lantern's average order value is R$ 170.33 one way and R$ 156.10 the other. What makes the first larger?

choices.text: A rounding difference between the two queries
choices.why: Fourteen reais is not rounding.

choices.text: The second excludes refunded orders
choices.why: Both use the same rows.

choices.text: Frequent large buyers weigh more per order
choices.why: Right. In the ratio of sums each order counts once, so offices with many large orders pull it up.

choices.text: The first counts the test account's one-cent orders, which lowers the second instead
choices.why: Both exclude customer 1.

prompt: Match each question to the kind of average that answers it.

pairs.left: what does an order bring in, on average?
what does a typical customer spend per order?

prompt: A dashboard shows "conversion" as the average of 533 daily conversion rates. Which kind of average is that, and what does it weight?

choices.text: A ratio of sums, weighting each visit
choices.why: That would divide total purchases by total visits.

choices.text: An average of ratios, weighting each day
choices.why: Right. A quiet January day counts as much as a busy May one; the shop's conversion is the ratio of sums.

choices.text: A median, weighting nothing
choices.why: A mean of rates is not a median.

choices.text: A weighted average by visits
choices.why: Averaging the daily rates gives every day the same weight.

prompt: Why do almost a third of Lantern's orders fall on a different day in UTC than in São Paulo?

choices.text: Because UTC skips the daylight saving hour
choices.why: The offset is the cause, not a skipped hour.

choices.text: They are placed after 21:00 local time, which is past midnight UTC
choices.why: Right. 2,278 of 7,102 orders, and São Paulo is three hours behind.

choices.text: Because the database stores local times without a zone
choices.why: It stores `timestamptz`, which is what makes either day possible.

choices.text: Because orders are timestamped when they ship
choices.why: The table records when the order was placed.

prompt: Monday 4 May 2026 has 42 orders in São Paulo days. How many does it have in UTC days?
In UTC the quarter has one order fewer and R$ 214.60 more. How can it have fewer orders and more money?

choices.text: Some orders are counted in reais in UTC
choices.why: Units do not change with the clock.

choices.text: The UTC query includes refunds
choices.why: Both queries are the same except for the zone.

choices.text: Different sales leave at one edge and arrive at the other
choices.why: Right. What remains is the net of the crossings: the orders that leave and those that arrive are not the same size.

choices.text: PostgreSQL rounds money differently in UTC
choices.why: Cents are integers in both.

prompt: What does a `timestamptz` column make possible that a timestamp without a zone does not?

choices.text: Storing dates before 1970
choices.why: Both types can.

choices.text: Choosing the day boundary at query time
choices.why: Right. A local time with no zone has already made the choice, and nobody wrote down which.

choices.text: Saving space
choices.why: Not the lesson's point.

choices.text: Automatically converting every value to the user's own browser time zone in every tool
choices.why: It converts to the session's zone, which you set.

prompt: Put the lines of the bridge in the order the lesson builds it.
items: minus refunded orders, at their net value
trap: Refunds before discounts is the usual slip: then refunds must be taken at gross, or the discount on them is removed twice.

prompt: Why is the bridge's last line computed on its own rather than as the sum of the lines above it?

choices.text: Because PostgreSQL cannot sum a `UNION ALL`
choices.why: It could, in an outer query.

choices.text: To make the query shorter
choices.why: It makes it longer.

choices.text: So that a gap in the bridge would show
choices.why: Right. A total built from its own steps always closes and can hide a missing difference.

choices.text: Because finance requires the net figure to be typed in by a person
choices.why: Nothing is typed; it is computed independently.

prompt: "Minus the test account: 0.00." Why keep a line of zero?

choices.text: It shows the exclusion was checked this quarter
choices.why: Right. A missing row says nothing, and next quarter the row may matter.

choices.text: Because removing it would change the total
choices.why: It is zero; the total would not move.

choices.text: Because `UNION ALL` requires five rows
choices.why: It takes any number.

choices.text: Because the test account has an open refund
choices.why: Nothing says so.

prompt: In the bridge for the first quarter of 2026, how many reais of refunded orders are removed?
Which row of the definition card is the one most cards leave out and most readers need?

choices.text: The formula
choices.why: Formulas are rarely left out.

choices.text: The owner
choices.why: Important, but not the row the lesson singles out.

choices.text: Known caveats
choices.why: Right. It is where lesson 1's findings reach the person reading the chart.

choices.text: The grain it can be shown at, because tools pick it on their own
choices.why: Useful, but not the one singled out.

prompt: Last week's net revenue was R$ 21,000 on Monday and R$ 20,600 on Friday, with no data error. What explains it?

choices.text: The time zone was changed between the two readings
choices.why: Nothing says so, and the definition fixes it.

choices.text: Refunds arrived for orders placed that week
choices.why: Right. Refunds are known only when they happen, which is why the card warns that a recent period can still fall.

choices.text: Integer division rounded the discounts differently on Friday
choices.why: Rounding is deterministic.

choices.text: The test account placed orders
choices.why: That would be excluded, not subtracted later.

prompt: What does `COMMENT ON VIEW` give a definition that a document on a shared drive does not?

choices.text: Enforcement: queries that ignore it fail
choices.why: A comment enforces nothing.

choices.text: Version history
choices.why: A comment holds only its current text.

choices.text: Translation into every language
choices.why: Not a feature of comments.

choices.text: It travels with the view
choices.why: Right. Whoever opens the database finds the definition beside the arithmetic.

prompt: A team rewarded for orders raises them with coupons that cost more than the orders bring. What is this an instance of?

choices.text: Goodhart's law
choices.why: Right. When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.

choices.text: A confounder, because coupons and orders share a cause in the segment
choices.why: The coupons cause the orders here; nothing hidden drives both.

choices.text: A lagging metric being read too early
choices.why: Timing is not the problem; the target is.

choices.text: Simpson's paradox
choices.why: Nothing reverses across groups here.

prompt: Match each target to the guardrail the lesson pairs it with.
Which of these is a leading metric for Lantern?

choices.text: Net revenue for last quarter
choices.why: Known only when nothing can change it: lagging.

choices.text: This week's share of visits reaching the checkout
choices.why: Right. It moves first and can still be acted on.

choices.text: Customers who ever ordered
choices.why: It only grows and leads nothing.

choices.text: Last year's refund rate
choices.why: Lagging by a year.

prompt: Finance starts counting refunds on the refund date instead of the order date. What does the lesson require?

choices.text: Recompute every past report under the new rule so history is consistent
choices.why: The old version stays readable; last year's report was computed under it.

choices.text: A new dated version, with the old one kept
choices.why: Right. And a chart crossing the date says so, or the step reads as something customers did.

choices.text: Edit the view and tell nobody, since the numbers improve
choices.why: A silent edit is what the lesson forbids.

choices.text: Keep both definitions under the same name
choices.why: That recreates the meeting the lesson is about.

prompt: A colleague's "revenue" for March is higher than finance's. Which of these could explain the difference? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Refunded orders are included
choices.why: Right. A filter difference.

choices.text: Gross values are summed instead of net
choices.why: Right. A measure difference.

choices.text: Days are cut in UTC
choices.why: Right. A time difference, which can move orders across the month's edges.

choices.text: The colleague used `sum` and finance used `sum`
choices.why: The same aggregation explains nothing.

prompt: Marketing wants "active customers" to count anyone who opened a Lantern e-mail in the last 30 days. What is the strongest objection?

choices.text: E-mail opens cannot be counted in SQL
choices.why: Anything recorded can be counted.

choices.text: The window should be 31 days
choices.why: The window is the smaller issue.

choices.text: It counts an action that says little about buying
choices.why: Right. Which action counts is part of the definition, and a weaker action gives a larger, less meaningful number.

choices.text: Marketing is not allowed to own metrics
choices.why: Any team can own a metric; this one is defined poorly.
